summary: This document adds a small number of mandatory tests needed for secure IKEv2 operation with elliptic curve groups. Implementations using modular exponential groups need no change except for a few rarely used DSA groups. It updates the IKEv2 protocol, RFC 5996.

plainLanguage.summary: When two computers mix numbers to make a secret, they must check the numbers are not sneaky. This adds those checks.

questions: why validate diffie-hellman public values in ikev2
do ikev2 peers need to check elliptic curve points
what happens when an ikev2 key exchange payload fails validation
subtitle: Extra sanity checks IKEv2 peers must run on a received Diffie-Hellman public value, so reused keys cannot be attacked.

tldr.problem: IKEv2 does not require a peer to test the Diffie-Hellman public value it receives. For elliptic curve groups, and a few other groups, a peer that reuses its DH values across sessions can leak information about its private key.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a validity test for each type of DH group (range checks for modular groups, a curve-equation check for elliptic curve groups), says what to do when a test fails, and describes a timing attack with a blinding-factor countermeasure.
tldr.outcome: The tests are RECOMMENDED for everyone and REQUIRED for implementations that reuse DH private keys. The RFC updates RFC 5996 and adds a Recipient Tests column to the IANA registry.

facts.label: EC curve equation
facts.value: y^2 = x^3 + ax + b mod p

today: RFC 6989 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2013 that updates RFC 5996. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Gap in IKEv2
sections.content:
IKEv2 (RFC 5996) sets up a shared secret with the Diffie-Hellman (DH) protocol and then authenticates the two peers. IKEv2 does not require the peer that receives a DH public key to run any tests on it. That is fine for the common modular exponential (MODP) groups, such as those in RFC 3526. For other groups, when peers reuse DH values across several IKE sessions, the missing tests are a potential vulnerability. The RFC singles out Elliptic Curve (EC) groups, whose use was growing.

The document defines tests for several types of DH group. It also describes a timing attack on reused DH keys, with material taken from RFC 2412. It updates RFC 5996 by adding security requirements that apply to many implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: When two computers agree on a secret, nobody was checking whether the number they received made sense. This RFC adds that check.

sections.title: Group Membership Tests
sections.content:
The tests apply to the recipient of a Key Exchange (KE) payload. They are RECOMMENDED for all implementations but REQUIRED for those that reuse DH private keys. Which test applies depends on the group:

  • Sophie Germain prime MODP groups (where (p-1)/2 is also prime): the recipient MUST check that the peer's public value r is in range, 1 < r < p-1. Even then a single bit of the secret exponent may leak when keys are reused, which the RFC calls insignificant.
  • MODP groups with small subgroups (those of RFC 5114, where (p-1)/2 is composite): the implementation MUST pick one of two options. Either check the range and also that r^q = 1 mod p, where q is the subgroup size, in which case DH private values MAY be reused; this suits NIST 800-56A conformance. Or never reuse private values (each one MUST come from a fresh output of a cryptographically secure random number generator) and check the range.
  • Elliptic curve groups over GF(p): the recipient MUST check that the x and y values of the peer's public value satisfy the curve equation y^2 = x^3 + ax + b mod p. For groups 19, 20 and 21, a = -3 (mod p). No check for the point at infinity is needed, because IKE cannot encode it.

The small-subgroup test is costly, roughly as expensive as what reusing DH values saves, which is why the second option exists.
sections.plainLanguage: Before using a number a stranger gave you, you check it is in the allowed range, or that it really sits on the right curve. Some number types need a bigger check than others.

sections.title: What to Do When a Test Fails
sections.content:
A recipient whose test fails must assume the sender is either truly malicious or has a bug. During IKE_SA_INIT, it MUST drop the message with the invalid KE payload and MUST NOT use it to create the IKE security association. With the DoS-resistant behavior of RFC 5996, it may simply ignore the message and keep waiting for a legitimate one. Without it, an invalid payload in the request lets the implementation MAY send an INVALID_SYNTAX notification and remove the half-built SA; in a response it MAY delete the SA and start again.

After the IKE SA exists, such as in CREATE_CHILD_SA, a Responder receiving an invalid KE payload in a request MUST reply with INVALID_SYNTAX and drop the IKE SA. An Initiator that gets an invalid payload in a response MUST immediately delete the IKE SA with a Delete notification in a new exchange. Dropping the SA makes the peer's bug easier to detect.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone hands you a suspicious number, you toss that message out. Once a trusted conversation is already running, you end it, because the other side clearly has a problem.

sections.title: The Timing Attack and Blinding
sections.content:
Besides the small-subgroup attack there is a potential timing attack when peers reuse DH secret values. It is a side-channel attack, so whether it is a real vulnerability depends on implementation details and the threat model. The RFC quotes RFC 2412 here and notes the attack applies to IKEv2 with both MODP and ECDH groups.

One countermeasure is a blinding factor. The implementation picks a random group element r and computes its inverse r_inv modulo p. Instead of computing (g^y)^x directly, it computes A = r*g^y, then B = A^x, then C = B*r_inv^x, which equals g^(xy). This hides the real sequence of operations. The blinding factor is only necessary if the exponent x is used more than 100 times.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone can time how long your math takes, they might guess your secret. Mixing in a random disguise number first, then removing it, hides the real timing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC gives an attack the tests prevent. Alice keeps IKE SAs with Bob and Eve and uses the same secret ECDH key for both. Without the tests, Eve can send a malformed public key that lets her efficiently work out Alice's private key, and so obtain Alice's shared IKE SA key with Bob.

Keys can be reused in different ways: for the same and for different peers, for the same peer only, or only when a key was not used to complete an exchange (for example after an INVALID_KE_PAYLOAD reply). The small-subgroup and timing attacks apply at least to the first two patterns.

Groups not covered, such as even-characteristic elliptic curves with cofactors greater than 1, may leak information. A document defining such a group MUST describe the tests it needs. The error notification for a failed test is safe because the groups are public and the tests use no private key, but in IKE_SA_INIT it is unauthenticated and only useful for debugging.
sections.plainLanguage: If you reuse the same secret with two people and do not check what they send, a bad one can trick you into giving away the secret you share with the other.

sections.title: IANA Registry Changes
sections.content:
IANA added a column named "Recipient Tests" to the Transform Type 4 (Diffie-Hellman Group Transform IDs) registry for IKEv2. It maps each group number to the section of this RFC that gives its test. Groups 27 to 30 are defined in RFC 6954.

Future documents that define new DH groups for IKEv2 are REQUIRED to provide this information for each new group, possibly by referring to this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of groups gained a new column that says which safety check each group needs.
